thread.title: Is Elon Musk the Only Thing Standing Between Tesla and an Industry Changing Partnership? - Barron's

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Is Elon Musk the Only Thing Standing Between Tesla and an Industry Changing Partnership? - Barron's
text:
By Teresa Rivas Updated Aug. 13, 2018 12:02 p.m. ET Shares of Tesla (TSLA) are lower on Monday, as the go-private saga rumbles on.
Where we were : Tesla shares have been volatile ever since CEO Elon Musk surprised markets with his plan to take the electric car maker private last week.
Where we're headed ...is still anyone's guess right now. But it'll likely remain a wild ride.
Illustration: JOHANNES EISELE/AFP/Getty Images) It may be mid-August, but there are few dull moments when it comes to Tesla (TSLA).
There has been plenty of volatility in the shares related to numerous questions about CEO Elon Musk' s plan to take the electric car maker private , which Barron's warned could be a sign of trouble to come . In fact, in just the past few days, which includes the weekend, we've heard how the deal complicates its debt , may not be easy to execute with regard to current shareholders , has sparked lawsuits (along with a government probe ), and may include funding from Saudi Arabia (which could complicate it from a national security standpoint).
Yet Tesla's board of directors is taking the go-private idea seriously, so markets can't ignore the possibility, however fraught it may be.
There's no shortage of thoughts on Tesla and the plan today. Oppenheimer's Colin Rusch writes that all the drama has taken investor focus off the fundamentals. Yet it's important not to lose sight of the actual deliveries: It's estimated that July saw 14,250 Model 3 shipments more than twice the May and June estimates, which "would translate into strong operating cash flow, should Tesla hit gross margin targets."
However, the Models S and X US shipment estimate came in at 2,525, not far above the 2,350 Tesla logged in April, which suggest a "limited pickup in shipments." Rusch writes that he expects "concerns around depth of demand for Models S and X to linger, supporting an important argument of the bear case."
As for Tesla's debt, Moody's Investor Service's Bruce Clark argues that the go-private plan would be credit negative, and potentially leave current bondholders exposed. Moreover, "whether Tesla remains public or private, the company faces substantial challenges" that indicate it will need to return to capital markets to fund operations and meet debt requirements.
New Street Research's Pierre Ferragu doesn't think it'll happen at all: "Doing our best with the limited information we have, we come to the conviction that Tesla is unlikely to go private, and anticipate the board will reject Elon Musk’s offer or approach."
But as Ferragu writes, we just still don't have much information to go on. Datatrek's Nicolas Colas writes that "If Musk really has his capital ducks in a row, then the strategic implications of the transaction are minimal. If he doesn’t, there is ample room for a broad range of partnerships that fundamentally remake the auto industry."
Those partners could include anyone from Apple (AAPL) to Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) on the tech side to Ford (F) to Fiat Chrysler (FCAU) among big automotive players, all of which could likely see strategic benefit from partnering with Tesla. Yet as Colas notes, "when you buy into Tesla, you get Elon Musk." Any potential suitor will have to decide if that's a bonus or just baggage.
Tesla is down 1.3% to $350.90 this morning.
